s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j.title: The nodes are the specification
s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j.text:
The specification is the set of its nodes.

Whatever is generated from the nodes — a readable export (for example, in markdown), the map, the instructions an agent reads — is regenerated after every change to them. It is never edited. Nothing is ever read back from it into the specification.

What is generated from the nodes into the system's code — its types and RuntimeChecks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and what a project's own generators write (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) — waits for its nodes instead. It is regenerated only once every node it is generated from is approved. Until then, no commit changes it.

Where a generated copy is kept, it is checked against what the nodes produce, unless it waits.
s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j.reason:
A copy that is edited, fed back into the nodes or left behind them would be a second version of the rules. Sooner or later one version would change and the other would not. Whoever read the unchanged one would then implement a rule that no longer holds.

A readable copy is needed all the same, because a structure a schema can check is hard for a person to read. Regenerated by the tools at every change and checked against the nodes, a copy is a view of the one source rather than a second one.

Code generated from a node is part of the system. Regenerated from a draft node, it would implement what none of the node's owners has approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). Waiting, it lets a change to the node be committed before its approval, as a change to any rule is. Since no commit changes it meanwhile, it is still never edited.

A copy that waits is left behind its nodes only until every one of them is approved. Meanwhile its lag is reported (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), so that nobody takes it for current.
doubts: Both lists set off by dashes (what is generated; what is generated into the code) are kept as dashes, so as not to decide whether they are examples or the whole set.

s-eferktypcj7njt5.title: The structure of the specification is defined by its schema
s-eferktypcj7njt5.text:
The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its schema. That schema is the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines, with the extension a project's own guidelines add to it.

The extension changes no definition the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds. It may add only:

- NodeKinds (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2);
- properties of an existing NodeKind, which the nodes of the SpecSheriff guidelines need not hold;
- properties of a file or of a link.

A file that does not match the schema is refused. The refusal names the property that is wrong.

Why each part of the structure is as it is, is written in the schema beside it.
s-eferktypcj7njt5.reason:
A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing. Stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. The schema is therefore the only description of the structure. A rule that names a part of it, to say what that part means, is compared with the schema by machine.

A project needs NodeKinds, and properties of nodes, of files and of links, that the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee. They are held as the shared ones are only where they stand in the schema every file is checked against. An extension that changes no definition of the shared schema keeps every structure the SpecSheriff guidelines define the same in every project. So a tool or a reader relying on one of those structures is never wrong there.
doubts: "the field that is wrong" became "the property that is wrong", taken as a field of the node schema; if it meant a field of a RecordType, it should go back.
s-eferktypcj7njt5.split: The limits of a project's extension, and the requirement that the schema states beside each part why it is so, can each be carried out apart from the schema defining the structure and refusing a file.

s-7445ahgjck2aefg.title: A node is one rule, and a section holds rules
s-7445ahgjck2aefg.text:
One numbered rule is one node. Its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks belong to that node rather than standing beside it.

A section is a container of rules. Its text states what the section is responsible for. The text requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule.

A section holds at least one rule, where:

- a RecordType, a term node or a node of a project's own NodeKind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) counts as one;
- the rules of the sections inside it count as its own.

A section whose rules have all gone is deleted. Every link and citation naming it is moved to the node that now holds its matter, or removed.
s-7445ahgjck2aefg.reason:
A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would invent a second set of locations for fragments nothing can cite.

A requirement written into a section's text is a rule nobody can cite, name in a SpecTag or check on its own. A section with no rule states a responsibility nothing in the code answers to.

A RecordType, a term node and a node of a project's own NodeKind each state on their own what must hold, as a rule does. A RecordType states the shape of its data. A term states what its word means in every rule that uses it. A node of a project's own NodeKind states what its NodeKind is declared for. Each is cited by its sid and named by SpecTags, so a section holding one holds a requirement.
s-7445ahgjck2aefg.split: That one rule is one node with its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks; and what a section is, holds and how it is deleted.

s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx.title: A node is cited by its sid, and its location names where it is in the specification
s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx.reason:
A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes. A specification that grows is reordered, and its rules move between domains, for as long as it grows. A sid is not a place. Moving a node changes its location, never its sid, so no reference holding the sid breaks.

The location stays where a person reads, computed so that it can never disagree with where the node is.
s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx.split: The sid, given once and cited everywhere; and the location, computed by the numbering given here.

s-5ah25f6gy99panq.title: What a node's status says
s-5ah25f6gy99panq.reason:
An approved status claims that one of the node's owners agreed to what it now states. A status that survived a rewrite would certify words nobody approved. A draft node asks for no code (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). It tells its owners that it waits for their approval.

A change of owners changes who reads a part, not what a rule states. An owner leaving, or a node moving, takes back nothing that was agreed. Links, metadata and what is built from other nodes are not what an owner approved. They change as the specification grows around a rule.

A withdrawal gives no agreement in anyone's name. It only makes a node a draft, as a change to its wording by anyone does. So whoever finds an approved rule wrong can keep any further change to its code or its tests from being committed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owners. The withdrawal names whoever made it, which tells the owners whom to ask.

A project takes the SpecSheriff guidelines as they were approved where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), so their approval is not the project's to withdraw. Whether the rule that approves the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold all code and tests. That is the specification's owners' choice (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).
doubts: "Anyone may withdraw the approval of a node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes, but that of the rule that approves the specification" was read as two exceptions to "anyone may" and written as a list; the reason supports that reading.
s-5ah25f6gy99panq.split: Who may withdraw an approval, and whose approval nobody but its owners may withdraw, could stand apart from what the status means and what keeps it.

s-9kfdycuq34beqvs.title: The status of a section and of a domain's header
s-9kfdycuq34beqvs.text:
The status of a section is built from the nodes under it that are no section. It is `approved` where every one of them is approved, and `draft` otherwise. The status of a domain's header is built the same way from every node of the domain but the header itself.

Nobody approves a section or a header itself, nor a header's level and where its code is.

The status is built anew after every change to the specification. It is never written by hand.
s-9kfdycuq34beqvs.reason:
A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg, §s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr). What they state, the nodes under them state, so their own words leave an owner nothing to agree to.

A header's level is one of those the project's own guidelines list (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4). The levels are listed in a rule the specification's owners approve. Where a header's code is says where to look, not what must hold.

Built from the nodes under it, the status shows at a glance which parts of the specification wait for their owners. Built anew after every change, it never falls behind those nodes (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

s-67vekyup7y8smap.title: Only its owners approve a node
s-67vekyup7y8smap.text:
The specification has owners, one or several. A domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) or a section may have owners of its own. They take the place of the owners above for every node within it.

A node is approved by one of its owners and by nobody else. An approval names whoever gave it.

An agent working for one of a node's owners approves the node in that owner's name where its wording changes only:

- to state what one of its owners approved in another node;
- by a replacement that changes no meaning, such as a renamed term or path.

The agent reports each such approval to that owner. The owner may withdraw it.
s-67vekyup7y8smap.reason:
An approval means that someone who answers for a rule has agreed to what it states, so it is theirs to give. Named, whoever approved is compared with the node's owners. A named approver can also be asked later.

Owners of domains and sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person reads. The owners of one part share its reading. Each of them answers for all of it.

A node whose wording only states what one of its owners approved in another node asks nothing its owners have not agreed to. A replacement that changes no meaning states nothing new. Shown again, either would spend the owners' attention on no choice.

An agent working for an owner already acts in that owner's name. It reports to them as it works. The report lets the owner see that the change was only that. Where it was not, the owner can withdraw the approval.
doubts: "spend the owners' attention on no decision" became "on no choice", taking "decision" in its ordinary sense.
s-67vekyup7y8smap.split: Who the owners are and that only they approve; and when an agent approves in an owner's name and reports it.

s-utvqbypzhmgndug.title: A draft node is not implemented
s-utvqbypzhmgndug.text:
A node is implemented only once it is approved.

Before a domain's implementation begins, the domain is reviewed whole. Where the implementation then finds a node silent or wrong, that node is changed and reviewed when the problem is found, not later.
s-utvqbypzhmgndug.reason: The specification is expected to be incomplete. Implementing a draft node fills its gap with a guess made in the code, which the specification then does not hold. Reviewing the node at once keeps the answer in the specification.
s-utvqbypzhmgndug.split: That only an approved node is implemented; and that a domain is reviewed whole before its implementation begins, a node found silent or wrong being changed and reviewed at once.

s-f2b5zvc565s242f.title: Removal goes through the archive when an approval was ever given
s-f2b5zvc565s242f.text:
A node an approval was ever given for is moved to the archive when it is removed. It goes there together with the reason for its removal and the sid of the node that replaces it, if one does.

A section, a domain's header and a node no approval was ever given for are deleted outright, whatever cited them.

A node may later be deleted from the archive.
s-f2b5zvc565s242f.reason:
A rule one of its owners approved is one the code may implement. A later change to its wording does not undo what was implemented from it, so its removal is worth keeping for a time. Kept in its last wording, it can be restored if its removal is undone.

An archived rule is also a record for the decisions taken. An approved rule that had to go, a rule of the base above all, most often shows a logic or an approach that was mistaken. Later work has to understand that logic or approach and take it into account, as it would a list of the defects found.

Nothing guarantees how long the archive keeps a node. So a link or a citation naming an archived node breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed.

A node no approval was ever given for was never implemented, since no SpecTag may name it. Archived, it would only bury the rules that had to go under wording nobody approved. A section and a domain's header require nothing, and nobody approves them (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs). So no code was implemented from them, and their removal keeps nothing worth restoring.
doubts: "a record for the decisions taken" kept: it is unclear whether it means the decisions of `meta.decisions` or choices in the ordinary sense, which would become "choices".

"breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed" kept in one sentence: it is unclear whether the checks refuse such a link from the archiving on or only once the node is deleted.

s-gqbj8849rf224qa.title: A decision lives on the rule it settled
s-gqbj8849rf224qa.text: A decision records what was settled about a rule. It is kept in that rule's `meta.decisions`, never as a document of its own. A decision usually changes the rule's wording. A procedural one changes none.
s-gqbj8849rf224qa.reason:
A decision is not specification but the history of one rule. It is read beside that rule. A procedural decision would otherwise leave no trace, because nothing in the wording shows it.

The number of decisions on one rule also measures how well it was written. A rule that keeps collecting them was written badly.

s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh.title: Work put off lives on the node it concerns
s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh.text:
Work put off that concerns one node is kept as an item of that node's `meta.todos`. It is never kept in a comment on the node or in a document of its own. A problem of the default implementation set aside is a rule of the technical debt instead (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

An item holds the day the work was put off, who its author is and what is to be done. An item is removed once it is done or given up.

Every item of `meta.todos` across the specification can be listed at once, the newest first, each with the node it stands on.
s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh.reason:
Work put off is read beside the node it concerns, as a decision is, so whoever opens the node sees what still waits on it. Kept in a comment or a document, it is missed by the listing.

An item's date orders the listing. Its author tells the reader whom to ask. An item left once done or given up shows work waiting that no longer waits.

Listed together, the items show what waits across the specification. The newest stand first: each older item was weighed at every listing since, a new one at none.
s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh.split: Where work put off is kept and what an item holds; and the listing of every item across the specification, the newest first.

s-dpe5kcz4eamv39g.title: A rule and its reason are held apart
s-dpe5kcz4eamv39g.text:
A node's text states what must hold. A rule of the technical debt is the exception: its text describes a problem as it stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

Why a node's text must hold is kept in a separate property of the same node. What that property holds is not part of the requirement.

When a rule is revised, its reason is checked first. A rule whose reason no longer holds is removed, not reworded.
s-dpe5kcz4eamv39g.reason:
Mixed in one text, a rule is long. A reader cannot tell which half of it is being asserted.

A reason that has stopped holding is the surest sign the rule should go. Nobody sees that sign while the reason is buried inside the requirement.
s-dpe5kcz4eamv39g.split: That the text and the reason stand in separate properties; and that a revision checks the reason first, removing a rule whose reason no longer holds.

s-efe2cmw9asrbt2g.title: What the specification governs
s-efe2cmw9asrbt2g.text:
The specification describes the system: its logic, its architecture and everything the system is made of. It governs one process only: how the specification itself is kept, changed and implemented.

A rule is dropped where it:

- tries to govern anything else;
- states the obvious.
s-efe2cmw9asrbt2g.reason:
A rule governing what nobody here controls decides nothing. An agent that has never read an instruction cannot be stopped by it, however many are written. Duplication and drift are fought by structure — one model, a generated export, links a checker resolves — not by prohibitions.

A rule stating the obvious costs a reading and decides nothing either.

s-xqs2e24mx5253ye.title: The specification holds its content, and the code implements it
s-xqs2e24mx5253ye.text:
The specification holds its content and the code implements it, never the reverse.

A rule does not hand what it states to a declaration in the code. A set of states, a list of members, a table of routes is described in the specification. The code is checked against that description.

A rule that sends its reader to a source file for its content is a defect. It is repaired when that rule is revised.
s-xqs2e24mx5253ye.reason:
A specification that leaves a list in the code and names only its meaning cannot say what the system is. A copy of that list written beside it in prose goes stale with nothing noticing.

Held in the specification and checked against the code, the content is in one place, and the disagreement is found by a machine.

s-v7vd4ydrwexsgsj.title: A member of `TextRule.list` may be an object
s-v7vd4ydrwexsgsj.text: Each member of `TextRule.list` is a primitive value or an object. In an object, the property the list names holds the member's value. The object's other properties hold what is stated of that value, each of them a primitive value, a list or an object.
s-v7vd4ydrwexsgsj.reason: What is stated of a value, held in that value's own object, is never taken for what is stated of another. The named property stays where the value is declared. So the members are read, and compared with their declaration, the same whatever else they hold.
doubts: "the property the list names" kept as words: it is the list's own part `property`, which RULES.md does not name among the parts of `TextRule.list`.

s-5x737t9nee4zgaa.title: The base specification names no technology
s-5x737t9nee4zgaa.text:
A rule of the base specification states what the system does, never how the default implementation does it. It names no programming language, library, store, protocol, command or file path. How it is done, and any part of a rule that depends on it, is described in the technical appendix.

A technology may be named by example, in brackets, where the rule does not depend on it.
s-5x737t9nee4zgaa.reason: The same rules can then be implemented on another stack, with an appendix of its own, without editing a single rule. A rule that names its tools goes stale when they change, although what the system does has not.

s-xef48cjh6krvavz.title: Of a user interface the base states what it shows, not how it looks
s-xef48cjh6krvavz.reason: The same rules can then be given another look with an appendix of its own. A rule that names its look goes stale when the look changes, although what the user can rely on has not.

s-9hfbxv5pfnsh4kc.title: The base specification holds no figure of one instance
s-9hfbxv5pfnsh4kc.text:
The base specification holds no figure measured on an instance — a population, a rate, a duration observed there.

A threshold a rule needs is stated by the method an instance measures it with. Its value is a setting of the technical appendix.
s-9hfbxv5pfnsh4kc.reason: A figure belongs to the instance it was measured on and to the day it was measured. Every other instance would then pass or fail the rule by accident.

s-vj7ercem526zd6v.title: The technical appendix stands beside the base specification
s-vj7ercem526zd6v.reason:
The base specification stays stable while an implementation adapts to an instance's infrastructure and requirements, so only the technical appendix changes with an instance.

A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base binding nowhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too.

Read beside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts from what it copies.

How a rule is carried out has no other home, since the base names no technology. Described less exactly, it would leave a choice to whoever implements it. The code would then hold that choice, and the specification would not.

The appendix is no subject area of the system but the way every one of them is built, which no level can place. A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it. Divided as the base is, the implementation of a rule is looked for in one place.

The problems set aside are read as one list, so they stand in one section, which spans the domains as the stack does. A problem is not how a rule is carried out but where carrying it out falls short.

The repository holds nothing of any one instance, so what one instance chooses within the appendix is a setting, not a rule.
doubts: "A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it" kept: it is unclear which of the two is read beside the other.
"in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation —" became a colon; the three are still read as what that detail is.
s-vj7ercem526zd6v.split: What the appendix is and the sections it holds; that it never contradicts the base; that each of its nodes describes and implements nodes of the base; and that an instance changes it for itself, through settings with their defaults.

s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw.title: The technical debt holds the problems of the default implementation set aside
s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw.reason:
A problem set aside needs a place where it is stated, or it is forgotten, or kept as a task nobody means to do. Every problem there stands for the one reason that the specification's owners judged it not worth solving now. So a reason or a decision of its own would only repeat its standing.

Described as it stands and bound to the nodes it concerns, a problem tells whoever repeats an instance, or reads those nodes, what the implementation does not do. Left standing once solved, it would describe a shortfall that no longer exists.

A problem in a technology may be solved by a later version of it while nothing here changes. The version it was seen in lets a reader tell.
doubts: "the decision to set the problem aside" became "the choice", taking it in its ordinary sense; "no decision records it" stays, being an item of `meta.decisions`.
